reader_message: How are Alice's size changes connected to her sense of who she is?

book_evidence.text: “Who are _you?_” said the Caterpillar. This was not an encouraging opening for a conversation. Alice replied, rather shyly, “I—I hardly know, sir, just at present—at least I know who I _was_ when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been changed several times since then.”

“Oh, I’m not particular as to size,” Alice hastily replied; “only one doesn’t like changing so often, you know.” … “Well, I should like to be a _little_ larger, sir, if you wouldn’t mind,” said Alice: “three inches is such a wretched height to be.”

draft.reply: In Chapter 5, Alice tells the Caterpillar she hardly knows who she is, because she has changed several times since she got up. Later, she says she dislikes changing so often and wants to be a little taller, grounding the identity question in her immediate experience of her body. What part of that connection stands out to you?
